Fit and rank candidate distributions

Source: R/dstfit.R
dstfit.Rd

Fits candidate distributions to one numeric variable by maximum likelihood, ranks them by AIC, and reports for each the BIC, a Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance, an Anderson-Darling statistic and percentile bootstrap intervals for its parameters. A Hill estimate of the tail index is added for positive data. Everything is base R.

Usage

dstfit(x, fams = NULL, nboot = 200L, conflvl = 0.95, seed = 1L, k = NULL)

# S3 method for class 'rmbl_dstfit'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

x

Numeric vector, the variable.

fams

Character vector of families (see Details), or NULL for every family the data allow.

nboot

Whole number, default 200: bootstrap resamples (0 for none).

conflvl

Number in (0, 1), default 0.95: the bootstrap and Hill interval level.

seed

Whole number, default 1: the seed of the bootstrap.

k

Whole number or NULL: the upper order statistics of the Hill estimate.

object, ...

For print() and plot(): see plot.rmbl_dstfit().

Value

A list of class c("rmbl_dstfit", "list"):

table

data frame, one row per family ranked by AIC: rank, family, npar, loglik, aic, bic, ks, ad, converged and params (the estimates as text).

fits

named list of the estimates (named numeric vectors) of the converged fits.

boot

data frame: family, param, estimate, lower, upper (NA without a bootstrap).

hill

list: k, alpha, lower, upper, or NULL for data that are not all positive or fewer than ten values.

x, nmiss, discrete, conflvl

the data used, the count dropped, whether the data are counts, and the level.

Details

The families and their parameters: normal (mean, sd), lognormal (meanlog, sdlog), exponential (rate), gamma (shape, rate), weibull (shape, scale), t (location, scale, df: a location-scale Student t), pareto (xmin, alpha, with xmin the smallest value, its maximum likelihood estimate), beta (shape1, shape2) for proportions, and for counts poisson (lambda), negbin (size, mu), zip (pi, lambda) and zinb (pi, size, mu), the zero-inflated forms with pi the share of structural zeros. The normal, lognormal, exponential, Pareto and Poisson estimates are closed form; the negative binomial searches its size alone (its mu estimate is the mean); the rest are maximised by optim() on a log or logit scale, Nelder-Mead then BFGS.

With fams = NULL every family the data allow is fitted: for whole numbers of 0 or more the count families; otherwise the positive families for values above 0 (exponential for values of 0 or more) and beta for values strictly between 0 and 1; and normal and t always. A family named in fams that the data do not allow is refused. A fit that fails (the optimiser stops at a non-finite likelihood) is a row with converged = FALSE and no statistics.

AIC is \(2k - 2\ell\) and BIC \(k \log n - 2\ell\). The Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Anderson-Darling statistics use the fitted parameters, so their usual null distributions do not apply; they rank fits, they are not tests. The bootstrap resamples the data nboot times and refits; the interval is the percentile interval at conflvl. The Hill estimator uses the k largest values (default \(\lfloor\sqrt n\rfloor\)): \(\hat\alpha = k / \sum_{i \le k} \log(x_{(n-i+1)} / x_{(n-k)})\), with the asymptotic interval \(\hat\alpha (1 \pm z / \sqrt k)\).

Missing values are dropped and counted (nmiss). Errors: x not numeric, an infinite value, fewer than five values, all values equal, an unknown family or one the data do not allow. The bootstrap is seeded with seed for this call only; the session's random stream is left as it was.

References

Hill BM (1975). A simple general approach to inference about the tail of a distribution. Annals of Statistics 3, 1163–1174. doi:10.1214/aos/1176343247

Anderson TW, Darling DA (1954). A test of goodness of fit. JASA 49, 765–769. doi:10.1080/01621459.1954.10501232

See also

plot.rmbl_dstfit() for the density, QQ, PP and tail plots; mksyncol() with type = "fitted" for a synthetic sample from a fit.

Examples

set.seed(1)
x <- stats::rgamma(300, shape = 2, rate = 0.5)
f <- dstfit(x, nboot = 50)
f
#> Distributions fitted to 300 values, ranked by AIC
#> 
#>  rank      family npar loglik  aic  bic      ks      ad
#>     1     weibull    2 -673.5 1351 1359 0.02543  0.1965
#>     2       gamma    2 -674.3 1353 1360 0.03906  0.5088
#>     3   lognormal    2 -691.7 1387 1395 0.07364  3.4610
#>     4 exponential    1 -709.4 1421 1424 0.14763 13.0561
#>     5           t    3 -711.2 1428 1440 0.08261  3.4834
#>     6      normal    2 -717.2 1438 1446 0.09560  4.6589
#>     7      pareto    2 -945.7 1895 1903 0.36066 73.1955
#> 
#>   weibull      shape = 1.523, scale = 4.349
#>   gamma        shape = 2.0060, rate = 0.5125
#>   lognormal    meanlog = 1.095, sdlog = 0.812
#>   exponential  rate = 0.2555
#>   t            location = 3.686, scale = 2.283, df = 8.140
#>   normal       mean = 3.914, sd = 2.642
#>   pareto       xmin = 0.1680, alpha = 0.3474
#> 
#> Hill tail index 5.66 (2.97 to 8.35), from the 17 largest values
f$fits$gamma
#>     shape      rate 
#> 2.0061187 0.5125441 

# counts with extra zeros
n <- ifelse(stats::runif(300) < 0.3, 0, stats::rpois(300, 4))
dstfit(n, nboot = 0)$table[, c("family", "aic")]
#>    family      aic
#> 1     zip 1183.895
#> 2    zinb 1185.895
#> 3  negbin 1280.316
#> 4  normal 1382.649
#> 5       t 1384.649
#> 6 poisson 1448.838

# a family the data do not allow
try(dstfit(c(-1, 2, 3, 4, 5), fams = "gamma"))
#> Error : dstfit: `gamma` needs every value above 0
